Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

vignette:
Sione is a fifty-three-year-old airline pilot for a major Pacific carrier, married to Lani for nearly thirty years. His trauma began during a layover in a small, unstable island nation. He was taken by a militia group who suspected him of transporting intelligence cargo. For three days they held him in a concrete room with no windows. The guards beat him, deprived him of sleep, and forced him to listen to the crying of other prisoners held nearby. He could still summon the smell of that room-damp concrete, sweat, and the metallic tang of blood. What he came to dread most was the silence. When the guard on duty stopped talking, Sione knew something terrible was about to happen. The absence of sound meant the next beating was coming.

After he was rescued and returned home, Sione tried to resume his life. He went back to flying, but the cockpit no longer felt like a sanctuary. He caught himself checking the cockpit door lock four or five times before takeoff, running his hand over the handle to be sure. Unusual silence on the radio-a patch of empty air where there should have been chatter-made his chest tighten. He found himself scanning the cabin during boarding, watching every passenger's movements for signs that they might harm him. Crowded airports became a nightmare; he would arrive three hours early just to move slowly and keep his back to a wall. When a passenger cried during a turbulent landing, Sione felt his own eyes sting and his throat close. He had come to believe that if he saw someone cry, it meant he was back in that room, listening to another prisoner's sobs.

At home, Lani noticed the changes first. He checked every door and window before bed, sometimes twice. The silence of the house unsettled him, so the television ran all night. He could not tolerate a quiet evening. He had also begun to watch Lani more carefully-the way she moved, the tone of her voice-as if monitoring her for a threat he could not name. Their conversations grew shorter; he no longer wanted to go out to dinner or to family gatherings. The consequence was a growing distance between them, and Sione felt it but could not explain why he kept pulling away.

The memory of the concrete room returned without warning. During a long-haul flight, the smell of coffee or jet fuel would suddenly become the smell of damp concrete, and he would see the room in perfect photographic detail-the crack in the wall, the stain on the floor. The images were so vivid that he felt he was there. The emotion would hit him so hard he had to excuse himself to the lavatory, pressing his forehead against the cool metal door until the wave passed. On two occasions he felt so overwhelmed during descent that he had to hand control to his first officer without explanation, claiming nausea.

What finally brought him to seek help was an incident three weeks ago. A passenger refused to follow a flight attendant's instructions and began shouting, misbehaving loudly. For Sione, the man's aggression became the guards' threats. He felt a surge of terror and an overwhelming urge to flee the cockpit-to open the door and run, even thirty thousand feet in the air. He did not, but afterward he sat trembling, certain he had come close to doing something that would end his career. That evening he told Lani he needed to see someone.

Sione is afraid. He is afraid of losing his license, of being grounded, of being seen as weak. But he is also afraid of living the rest of his life in a state of constant watchfulness, checking locks and scanning faces, smelling concrete in the air. He hopes he can find a way to fly without fear, and to sit in a quiet room with his wife without feeling that danger is about to arrive.
